chose: Build it, tuned for browsing legibility rather than searchability
considered: Not building and relying on mdfind/Live Text indexing, which already finds these files by content on this machine
why: Human answered that Spotlight finds them fine and the real problem is browsing a folder of thousands of identical names; that reframes the quality bar from findable to scannable and removes search features from scope

chose: Mutate the original files with rename(2) in the same directory
considered: Hardlinking into a shadow directory; renaming plus leaving a symlink at the old name
why: Human chose in-place; it is what was asked for, preserves xattrs and Finder tags for free, and a second directory entry per file would defeat the legibility goal

chose: Do not scan for or rewrite references to renamed files
considered: Restricting the tool to files with no known referrer; building an Obsidian/Markdown link-rewrite pass
why: Human confirmed the corpus is an unreferenced Desktop junk drawer, so the longest-fuse failure mode does not apply and the undo journal is sufficient mitigation

chose: Ship both cloud and local backends, cloud as the default with --local as an explicit opt-in
considered: Cloud only; local only; local as the default with --cloud opt-in
why: Human chose both with cloud default: best names out of the box, accepting that screen contents go to an API unless --local is passed

chose: YYYY-MM-DD-content-slug.ext, lowercase kebab-case
considered: Including capture time; content-first with trailing date; slug with no date at all
why: Human chose the date-prefixed form; the prefix preserves chronological sort and acts as a uniqueness anchor so independently generated identical slugs do not collapse

chose: App-first: the application is the segment immediately after the date, subject segments follow
considered: Subject-first with app only as a disambiguator (the agent's recommended default); verbose full-sentence names
why: Human overrode the recommended default in favour of app-first, which is consistent with D-001: when search is already solved, a predictable leading token is what makes a large folder scannable

chose: Abstain and leave the original filename untouched
considered: Renaming with a generic marker such as -unclear; moving them into an unsorted/ subfolder
why: Human chose leave-untouched; abstaining is most of the perceived quality and it keeps the tool a renamer rather than a file mover

chose: ~/.local/state/shotname/ for cache, journal, and plan files
considered: A .shotname/ directory inside the target folder; cache in ~/.local/state with plan and journal in CWD
why: Human chose the XDG state directory: the target folder stays clean, iCloud does not sync tool state, and one journal location serves runs over different folders

chose: Skip files with SF_DATALESS set, report count and total nominal size, and provide --materialize to process them anyway
considered: Materializing automatically; prompting interactively once
why: Human chose skip-and-report but explicitly asked for a flag to materialize, so the tool never silently pulls gigabytes over a metered connection while still allowing full coverage on demand

chose: Python 3.12
considered: A Swift-native CLI; a Node CLI as ai-renamer does
why: The pyobjc binding to Apple Vision and the Anthropic SDK are both best-in-class in Python, and the tool is I/O-bound glue where language speed is irrelevant

chose: uv with pyproject.toml, installable and runnable via uvx
considered: pip with requirements.txt; Poetry; a standalone PyInstaller binary
why: Lockfile-backed and fast, and a single command installs a personal CLI without the user managing a virtualenv

chose: Typer
considered: argparse; Click directly
why: Subcommands and typed flags for free, and Click underneath means CliRunner-based testing of every flag-level acceptance criterion is standard practice

chose: ocrmac wrapping VNRecognizeTextRequest at .accurate recognition level
considered: The newer Live Text path; the macocr Swift CLI; ocrs as a cross-platform fallback; Tesseract
why: On-device, free, runs at native resolution before any downscaling, and returns per-line confidence and bounding boxes that the app-first rule uses to weight title-bar text; raised as Q-008 because Live Text reportedly extracts more

chose: Run on-device OCR first and send the extracted text alongside the downscaled image to the model
considered: Sending pixels straight to a vision model; tiling large screenshots instead of downscaling
why: Vision models downscale before they see the image, which is exactly the operation that destroys 11px UI text; both mature prior-art projects landed on OCR-first independently

chose: claude-haiku-4-5-20251001 on the standard resolution tier, overridable with --model
considered: A larger model; the high-resolution tier at roughly 3x the visual tokens
why: Cheapest model that is clearly good enough once OCR text carries the proper nouns; surfaced as Q-001 because the model choice is the entire bill and that is the human's money

chose: Ollama with llama3.2-vision as the default, overridable with --ollama-model
considered: LLaVA; Qwen-VL; Moondream; requiring the user to supply any model name with no default
why: Ollama is the common local runtime in the prior art and a named default means --local works without configuration; the backend interface makes the specific model swappable

chose: Tool-use / JSON schema on the model call, validated with Pydantic, retried once on validation failure
considered: Free-text response parsed with a regex; asking for a bare filename string
why: Turns a malformed response into a typed retry and then a recorded error rather than a silently wrong filename, and it is what makes the app and subject fields separable for the app-first rule

chose: SQLite in WAL mode keyed by content hash, storing OCR output and model output separately
considered: A directory of JSON files keyed by hash; caching inside the journal itself
why: Random-access lookup by hash across runs and safe concurrent writes from a worker pool; storing OCR and model results under separate keys lets a prompt change invalidate only the model half

decision: Journal substrate, separate from the cache
chose: Append-only JSONL fsynced per record before each rename
considered: Storing the journal in the same SQLite database as the cache
why: Undo must work even if the cache database is corrupt or deleted, and a plain-text journal is greppable and auditable by hand; deliberately two mechanisms, one with no moving parts

chose: Write and fsync the journal record before issuing rename(2)
considered: Writing the record after a successful rename; batching journal writes for throughput
why: The reverse order loses the record for exactly the file in flight when the process dies, which is the one file you most need to undo; a stale record for a rename that never happened is reconcilable, a missing one is not

decision: Content hash function and collision suffix
chose: BLAKE2b over file contents, first 6 hex characters as the disambiguation suffix
considered: SHA-256; a monotonic counter suffix; appending the capture time
why: Fast on large PNGs, and a truncated content-derived prefix is short enough for a filename and stable across runs, which is what makes collision suffixes reproducible

chose: Compare proposed names case-folded and NFC-normalized against both other proposals and existing on-disk files
considered: Byte-exact comparison; comparing only against other proposals in the run
why: APFS is case-insensitive and case-preserving by default and normalizes Unicode, so a byte-exact check would let stripe-dashboard.png silently clobber Stripe-Dashboard.png

chose: Renaming happens only with an explicit --apply, with no config or environment override
considered: Renaming by default with a --dry-run flag; an interactive confirmation prompt instead of a flag
why: At thousands of irreversible renames a bad prompt tweak is a catastrophe that cannot be eyeballed; making the safe path unconfigurable means it cannot be turned off by accident or by a stale shell alias

chose: Treat kMDItemIsScreenCapture as the primary signal, with the filename pattern as a secondary one and --all-images as an override
considered: Matching the Screenshot filename prefix only
why: The prefix is localized and user-configurable via defaults write, so filename matching alone misses German captures and any file the user already renamed; the Spotlight attribute is what Finder Stacks itself uses

chose: Match candidate filenames with a Unicode-aware whitespace class rather than a literal space
considered: A literal glob of the form Screenshot * at *.png
why: Since Sonoma the space before AM/PM is U+202F NARROW NO-BREAK SPACE, and a literal-space pattern silently matches nothing, which would make the tool appear to find zero files

chose: Enforce 255 bytes UTF-8 including the extension, truncating at a kebab-segment boundary
considered: A 255-character limit; a fixed 100-byte soft cap
why: The APFS limit is byte-based, so an accented or CJK name blows the limit well before 255 visible characters; truncating at a segment boundary keeps the name readable rather than cut mid-word

chose: Transliterate to ASCII and drop untransliterable characters
considered: Allowing NFC-normalized Unicode in filenames
why: Keeps every produced name safe in every shell, glob, and downstream tool, which is the class of bug this project exists to survive; surfaced as Q-006 since it does lose fidelity on non-Latin captures

chose: Non-recursive by default, --recursive to opt in, never following directory symlinks
considered: Recursive by default
why: The stated target is a single flat junk-drawer directory, and recursing by default into a home directory is how a rename tool does damage far outside what the user pointed it at

chose: Stream enumeration and processing so peak memory does not scale with the number of candidates
considered: Loading the full candidate list and all metadata into memory, which is fine at 4000 files
why: The 4000 figure is the current backlog, not a bound; treating it as a constant would silently cap the tool and would have to be undone the first time it is pointed at a larger archive

chose: asyncio with a bounded semaphore, default 8, settable with --concurrency
considered: A thread pool; firing all requests at once; fully serial processing
why: Both OCR and API calls are I/O-bound, and a bounded pool is what makes retry-after backoff, clean SIGINT, and honest progress reporting tractable at once

chose: Exponential backoff honouring the retry-after header on HTTP 429, with the file retried rather than errored
considered: Failing the file on 429; a fixed sleep interval
why: Rate limits are per-organization and a multi-thousand-file run will hit them; a 429 is a wait instruction, not a failure, and treating it as one would strand files mid-run

decision: Synchronous API rather than the Batch API in v1
chose: Synchronous requests with bounded concurrency
considered: The Batch API at 50% discount; a hybrid using batch for the full run and synchronous for samples
why: Low latency is what makes the sample-and-iterate loop usable and the full backlog still finishes in well under an hour; recorded as Q-002 because the 50% saving is the human's money to weigh against the added job-lifecycle machinery

decision: No corpus-level clustering pass in v1
chose: Name each file independently, relying on the date prefix and hash suffixes for uniqueness
considered: Re-prompting repeated slugs for specificity; a full near-duplicate clustering pass before naming
why: Keeps the pipeline streaming and the bill predictable; recorded as Q-004 because generic-name collapse is the single most likely reason the human dislikes the result and fixing it costs a second round of calls

chose: Abstain when OCR yields fewer than --min-ocr-chars (default 12) characters and image entropy is below threshold
considered: A more aggressive rule also keyed on model confidence and single-generic-segment names
why: The conservative rule almost never abstains on something nameable, which keeps the folder from ending up half-renamed; raised as Q-005 since the aggressive rule trades coverage for per-name quality

decision: Model refusals are an abstention, not a failure
chose: Record action abstain with reason model_declined, continue the run, and leave the exit code unaffected
considered: Treating a refusal as an error; retrying refusals with a modified prompt
why: Screenshots containing identifiable people will draw refusals as a matter of policy, so a refusal path that fails the run would break a multi-thousand-file job on entirely expected input

chose: --max-cost is opt-in with no default value
considered: A default ceiling around $15 that a run must exceed explicitly
why: A default ceiling would block legitimate large runs on a job whose expected cost is single-digit dollars; recorded as Q-007 because the protection it gives against a mistyped path is the human's call, not a technical one

chose: An alias map held as a data file, applied before slugification, with unknown apps slugified from the model's returned name unchanged
considered: Hard-coding the aliases in source; asking the model to normalize the app name itself
why: App-first naming only pays off if the leading token is stable, and a model asked to normalize will drift between runs; keeping the map as data means editing it is not a code change and determinism still holds

chose: 2 for missing API key, 3 for EPERM on the target directory, 130 for SIGINT, non-zero for undo with changed-content files
considered: A single non-zero exit code for all failures
why: Distinct codes let the tool be used in a script and make the TCC case, which is the most likely first-run failure, distinguishable from a configuration mistake

chose: On EPERM, print the literal System Settings path to grant Full Disk Access to the parent terminal application and exit, with no traceback
considered: Letting the OSError propagate; attempting to detect and request the permission programmatically
why: TCC blocks ~/Desktop and sudo does not help, so this is the most likely first-run failure and the error message is the entire user experience at that moment

chose: Use rename(2) within the same volume and never touch mtime or st_birthtime
considered: A copy-then-delete implementation, which would also permit moving files across volumes
why: Same-volume rename preserves extended attributes and Finder tags for free, while copy-delete drops them; and for a screenshot the capture timestamp is real information and is what sorts the folder

chose: --sample N selects a pseudo-random subset seeded by --seed with a fixed default, and never writes to disk even with --apply
considered: Taking the first N files; a fresh random subset on each invocation
why: Iterating on the prompt requires comparing runs over the same files, and the first N are chronologically clustered and unrepresentative of the corpus

chose: Print per-action counts, distinct-versus-total slug counts, duplicate slug count, name-length distribution, and 20 sampled rename pairs
considered: Printing only the counts of renamed and skipped files
why: Nobody can review thousands of names, so cheap statistical proxies are the only way the run's quality is measurable at all; duplicate slug count in particular is the direct readout on generic-name collapse

chose: Ship a built-in prompt, expose it with --print-prompt, and allow override with --prompt-template
considered: A fixed built-in prompt with no override
why: There is no ground truth for what a screenshot is about, so the naming instinct has to be the user's; the prompt-template version is part of the cache key so editing it correctly invalidates only cached model output

chose: pytest with pytest-asyncio, stubbed model calls, and a committed fixture corpus covering the known landmines
considered: Manual verification against the real screenshot folder; integration tests hitting the live API
why: Every acceptance criterion must be checkable without spending money or depending on one machine's file collection; the fixture corpus carries a U+202F name, a .PNG, a case-collision pair, a near-blank image, and a simulated dataless flag

chose: ruff for lint and format, mypy in strict mode
considered: black plus flake8; no type checking
why: Fast, single-tool, and no configuration debate; strict typing is worth it where the code manipulates paths and bytes that must not be confused with each other

decision: Naming model and resolution tier default
chose: Start on Haiku and let --sample decide
considered: Haiku 4.5 at the standard resolution tier; Haiku 4.5 at the high-resolution tier; Sonnet 5 at the standard tier; starting on Haiku and deciding from a sample
why: There is no way to know from a price table whether a downscaled screenshot is still nameable; a 30-file sample answers it against the actual corpus for cents. Makes model id and resolution tier per-run parameters rather than constants, so both enter the cache key, the cost estimate, and the completion report

chose: Batch API for the full run, synchronous for --sample
considered: Synchronous only with bounded concurrency; Batch API for the full run with synchronous --sample; Batch API only
why: The backlog is one-shot and latency-insensitive, so the 50% discount and the removal of rate-limit pressure are close to free, while the prompt-iteration loop is latency-bound and cannot wait on a job. Costs job-lifecycle code and makes the main run two-phase

chose: Both: --apply generates in one pass, --plan replays an approved plan
considered: Both paths supported; strict two-phase in which --apply requires --plan
why: Keeps the one-command path for runs already trusted while leaving the reviewed-plan path available; accepts that the one-pass form can rename files under names no human read, with the undo journal as the mitigation

chose: No corpus pass in v1; rely on the date prefix and hash suffixes
considered: No corpus pass; detecting repeated slugs and re-prompting those files for specificity; a full near-duplicate clustering pass
why: Keeps v1 streaming, cheap, and small. Accepts dozens of near-identical names differing only by date; the duplicate-slug count in the completion report is the instrument that would justify adding the pass later

chose: Conservative: abstain only on clearly empty images - under 12 OCR characters AND low entropy
considered: The conservative empty-image threshold; also abstaining on low model confidence or single-generic-segment names
why: A thin name beats a folder that is visibly half-renamed; low model confidence alone is explicitly not grounds to decline

chose: Transliterate to ASCII, drop what cannot be transliterated
considered: ASCII transliteration; NFC-normalized Unicode slugs within the 255-byte limit
why: Every filename stays safe in every tool and shell, and the tool avoids reintroducing the invisible-character and encoding class of bug it exists to survive; a Japanese-UI capture yields a romanized or generic name

chose: No default ceiling; --max-cost is opt-in
considered: No default ceiling; a default $15 ceiling overridable per run
why: Never blocks a legitimate large run; accepts that only the pre-run cost estimate stands between a mistyped path and a surprise bill

chose: Classic VNRecognizeTextRequest at .accurate via ocrmac
considered: Classic VNRecognizeTextRequest via ocrmac; the Live Text path with a classic fallback; benchmarking both on 50 real screenshots
why: Stable, documented, and the only option that returns the per-line confidence and bounding boxes the app-first slug rule depends on; accepts possibly extracting less text than Live Text on dark-mode or low-contrast captures

decision: Batch job lifecycle in the CLI
chose: A full run submits its jobs, records the ids under the state directory, and exits without renaming; re-invoking the identical command collects the results and continues, and --wait polls to completion within a single invocation
considered: Blocking on the batch by default; adding dedicated submit, status, and collect subcommands
why: Resolves the collision between the human's choice of the Batch API (D-047) and their choice that --apply generates in one pass (D-048). Re-invocation is already the promised resume path after SIGKILL and SIGINT, so batch collection rides on machinery the spec had already committed to instead of adding a second vocabulary; a batch can legitimately take up to 24 hours, which no foreground default should assume

decision: Batch request identity and job chunking
chose: custom_id is the file's content hash, and requests are split across jobs to stay under the provider's per-batch request-count and payload-size limits
considered: A per-run sequential id with a side table mapping ids back to paths; a single job per run
why: Keying on the content hash makes reconciliation independent of enumeration order and of whether a file was renamed between submission and collection, and collapses byte-identical duplicates into one paid request. Image payloads make the per-batch size limit, not the count limit, the binding constraint on a 4000-file backlog

decision: Escape hatch back to synchronous dispatch
chose: --sync forces a full run onto the synchronous endpoint, and the local Ollama backend always dispatches synchronously
considered: Making batch dispatch unconditional for every full cloud run
why: Batch is a cloud-backend concept with no local equivalent, so the backend interface must permit a synchronous full run; --sync also leaves a way to process a whole small corpus with immediate feedback when the discount is not worth the wait

decision: Whether to run "test-write" with the budget ceiling already spent
chose: park the project and hand the call back to the human
considered: run the stage anyway; abandon the project
why: budget: $10.52 spent of a $9.40 ceiling ($-1.12 left) — raise it with `sfo budget screenshot-content-renamer-fee869 <usd>` or take what is already built
